title: OPINION: Ukraine’s Black Soil and the Hidden Reality of a Ruined Country
content:
By Wolfgang Bittner*

GÖTTINGEN, Germany | 10 November 2026 (IDN) — Ukraine, which has been at war with Russia since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, is known for its fertile black soil—chernozem—a nutrient-rich humus soil that in some areas reaches considerable depth and produces high agricultural yields.

Chernozem covers a substantial part of Ukraine, particularly in the east and south. Ukraine possesses tens of millions of hectares of agricultural land and one of the world’s largest concentrations of black soil.

Ukraine is also the second-largest country in Europe after Russia. In recent years, its extensive mineral resources—including coal, iron ore, lithium, graphite, manganese, oil and natural gas—have increasingly become a subject of international interest.

Less attention is paid to the strategic importance of its agricultural land. Before the war, Ukraine was among the world’s leading exporters of corn and wheat and held important shares of global markets for barley, sunflower oil and rapeseed.

Before the full-scale war, Ukraine routinely produced around 60 million tonnes or more of grain annually, mainly corn, wheat and barley, with a large proportion exported.

title: There is No Clean Nuclear Bunker Buster
content:
Talk of a nuclear strike on Iran’s “Pickaxe Mountain” has no official basis. But if the idea resurfaces, the US National Academies settled the central question two decades ago: an earth-penetrating nuclear weapon cannot contain its effects.

By Tariq Rauf*

VIENNA | 9 November 2026 (IDN) — In recent days, parts of the US and international media have speculated that Washington might use a nuclear weapon against Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La (“Pickaxe Mountain”), the tunnel complex Iran reportedly is building inside a granite mountain about two kilometres south of its Natanz enrichment plant. To be clear at the outset: there is no official indication whatsoever that such a strike is contemplated or authorized. President Trump has said he would not use a nuclear weapon against Iran, and the weapon he has named for any attack on the site, the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, is conventional.

title: ESSAY: The Illusion of Decentralization: Cryptocurrency and the Contradictions of Digital Capitalism
content:
By Sam Ben-Meir*

NEW YORK | 7 November 2026 (IDN) — In a sophisticated cyberattack whose most intensive phase lasted approximately twenty minutes, hackers stole an estimated $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, in what investigators have described as the biggest digital asset theft in history.

The attack, whose precise mechanism remains under investigation, involved multiple points of breach and allowed hackers to transfer billions of dollars in digital assets into wallets under their control. Blockchain investigators have attributed the operation with high confidence to a North Korean hacking organization, although the investigation remains ongoing. Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals, pledged to cover customer losses, and coordinated with other cryptocurrency companies to freeze approximately $2.85 billion in affected assets.

title: OPINION: From the Strait of Hormuz to the Strait of Midterm, Trump Pays Heavy Price
content:
By Azu Ishiekwene

The writer is the Editor-In-Chief of LEADERSHIP and the author of the new book Writing for Media and Monetising It.

ABUJA, Nigeria | 7 November 2026 (IDN) — Those who voted for President Donald Trump and handed the Republicans a majority in the US Congress two years ago cannot claim it was a mistake. Twenty-two years ago, Dick Stoken wrote in The Great Game of Politics that there’s a psychology that explains why we elect whom we elect.

The midterm results just re-echoed Stoken’s point that the pendulum of US politics swings toward the middle all the time, not despite the voters, but because of them.

One Trump term (2017–2021) was enough. But because the Democratic Party had lost its way by creating a nanny state, compounding red tape, and deifying wokeism, Trump’s idiosyncrasies looked like middle ground. He was voted in again in 2024, despite his hubris.

title: OPINION: A UN for All? Asia’s Inclusion Must Be a Priority for the Next Secretary-General
content:
By Shihana Mohamed*

NEW YORK | 6 November 2026 (IDN) — “Outside these walls, people are not asking whether the United Nations still exists. They are asking whether it works.”

Khalilur Rahman of Bangladesh, President of the United Nations General Assembly, warned the international community in his opening remarks at the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA 81).

The theme of UNGA 81 was “Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all.” It was an attempt to repair a fracturing multilateral system and demonstrate the UN’s ability to deliver meaningful results for all.

However, statements by Asian leaders at the session highlighted several concerns. They questioned whether the UN can truly serve all nations effectively while significant inequalities persist in global decision-making.

At UNGA 81, Asia’s major powers called for reforms to global governance, challenging existing imbalances in representation and the distribution of global influence.

title: ESSAY: While the World Burns …
content:
By Franz Baumann*

This essay was originally published online on 2 November 2026 in Environment: Science and Policy for Sustainable Development, Taylor & Francis, under the title “While the World Burns …” DOI: 10.1080/00139157.2026.2725625.

VIENNA | 6 November 2026 (IDN) — “Our house is on fire while we avert our eyes. Nature, mutilated and plundered, can no longer regenerate and we refuse to admit it.”—President Jacques Chirac at the 2002 Earth Summit in Johannesburg, South Africa

Barry Commoner, the founder of Taylor & Francis Online, defined the Four Laws of Ecology in 1971:

Everything is connected to everything else. There is one ecosphere for all living organisms and what affects one, affects all.

Everything must go somewhere. There is no “waste” in nature and there is no “away” to which things can be thrown.

Nature knows best. Humankind has fashioned technology to improve upon nature, but such change in a natural system is likely to be detrimental to that system.

There is no such thing as a free lunch. Exploitation of nature will inevitably involve the conversion of resources from useful to useless forms.

title: OPINION: Iran: Compromise or Catastrophe
content:
By Alon Ben-Meir*

NEW YORK | 5 November 2026 (IDN) — There is no durable military solution to the American-Israeli conflict with Iran. Bombs can destroy installations, but they cannot erase scientific knowledge, extinguish national pride, or create a sustainable political settlement.

The choice is not between demonstrating strength and accepting weakness; it is between negotiating enforceable compromises and courting a catastrophe that could engulf the Middle East. Trump must recognize that understanding Iran’s history, security calculations, and determination to preserve its sovereignty is the indispensable starting point for diplomacy.

Trump’s fundamental failure has been to confuse overwhelming military power with an understanding of the adversary. Before negotiating with—or attacking—another country, a president must examine its history, national identity, geography, strategic military capabilities, resilience, and perception of existential threats. Understanding these factors does not excuse the Iranian regime’s repression or regional aggression. It makes American diplomacy and negotiation strategies more effective.

title: OPINION: African Countries Face Rising Economic Risks
content:
By Daniel D. Bradlow*

PRETORIA | 5 November 2026 (IDN) —The current global economic situation is confusing. On the one hand, it’s characterised by inflation and food and other critical supply shortages caused by the wars in Ukraine and the Gulf states. On the other, by optimism and economic growth caused by the boom in AI investments.

The situation both poses threats and offers opportunities to Africa.

On the upside, the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank are predicting that African growth will be around 4.5% in 2026 and 2027. This is higher than the IMF’s estimates of 3.1% global growth in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027.

The IMF maintains that African countries are reaping the rewards of the painful macro-economic reforms that they undertook earlier in the century. The reforms are helping African governments weather the shocks caused by the wars in Ukraine and the Gulf.

But the World Bank has warned that 2027 African poverty levels will be higher than they were in 2022. UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) reports that since 2010, the continent’s public debt has increased at about four times the rate at which its GDP has grown.

title: Sudan’s Empty Warehouses Leave Millions Without Shelter
content:
As relief stocks run out, expanding drone warfare, foreign arms supplies and divided diplomacy are worsening one of the world’s largest humanitarian emergencies

By Ramesh Jaura

BERLIN | 12 November 2026 (IDN) – Winter nights in Darfur and northern Sudan can be bitterly cold. Many families displaced by war are nevertheless sleeping beneath plastic sheets, in crowded public buildings or beside damaged houses.

Some have returned to their towns only to find that their homes have been destroyed or looted, water and electricity are unavailable and the nearest clinic is closed.

The UN Refugee Agency, UNHCR, and the International Organization for Migration, IOM, warned on 6 November that their stocks of tents, blankets and other essentials were almost exhausted. An estimated 15.4 million people need emergency shelter or basic household items, but available funds allow relief agencies to give priority to only about one in ten.

Even that reduced target has not been met. Only 936,000 people have received assistance.

Mohamed Refaat, head of IOM’s mission in Sudan, said the agency’s warehouses were empty. A convoy of 16 trucks that reached Darfur carried the last of its available stocks.

title: Russia Courts Africa but Investment Lags Behind Diplomacy
content:
Moscow has widened its political reach, but African governments want investment that creates jobs and reduces dependence as well as grain supplies and security agreements

By Kester Kenn Klomegah*

MOSCOW | 11 November 2026 (IDN) — African delegations came to Moscow for Russia’s third summit with the continent despite Western efforts to isolate the Kremlin. Their presence gave President Vladimir Putin a diplomatic success. The harder question is what African countries will receive from the agreements signed there: financing for factories, dependable electricity and jobs, or another round of promises.

The meeting on 28–29 October produced a cooperation programme for the next three years. But Russia’s political reach still exceeds its commercial presence. African governments can accept Russian offers while continuing to trade, borrow a|nd negotiate with Moscow’s competitors.

title: Beyond Endless Struggle: What The Battle of Algiers Still Teaches Us About Revolution
content:
By Sam Ben-Meir *

NEW YORK | 11 November 2026 (IDN) —In Paul Thomas Anderson’s One Battle After Another (2025), Leonardo DiCaprio’s character, Bob Ferguson, a disillusioned former revolutionary, watches Gillo Pontecorvo’s The Battle of Algiers (1966) on television. The juxtaposition is almost comical: a man whose revolutionary aspirations have collapsed into private survival contemplates one of cinema’s most powerful representations of collective struggle. Yet the scene raises a question Anderson’s film never fully confronts: What distinguishes a revolution capable of transforming the world from a rebellion condemned to repeat itself?

The juxtaposition is especially timely. On November 7, The Battle of Algiers was screened at the Brooklyn Academy of Music as part of Playback: The Brooklyn Watch Party, selected by actor John Turturro. Sixty years after its release, Pontecorvo’s film remains a challenge to the diminished revolutionary imagination of our time, insisting that resistance need not become perpetual repetition: even seemingly immovable structures of domination can be transformed.
